links.outcome: Retinal specialist over-reading of all AI-graded cases, including AI negatives
links.effect: Over-reading found 72 false positives among 201 AI referrals and 5/444 (1.1%) false negatives, 3 of which were severe NPDR; authors suggest over-reading may not be necessary given 88% concordance.
links.quote: This may imply that over-reading of AI results by expert human graders may not be necessary in implementing AI for DR screening but a mechanism to lower the unnecessary referral should be set up in a screening program.

links.outcome: Local AI agreement with specialist over-reader versus prior reported accuracy
links.effect: Concordance 88% (568/645); over-reader agreed with 64.18% of AI positives (129/201); about 35% unnecessary referrals and about 1% missed referrals, despite prior reported sensitivity and specificity >95%.
links.quote: Although the exact TP, TN, FP, and FN cases were not known without adjudication, there might be approximately 35% of cases which AI unnecessarily referred and approximately 1% of cases which AI missed referral, according to the specialist.

links.outcome: Missed referrals identified through specialist review of AI-negative cases and subsequent referral attendance
links.effect: Specialist over-reading identified 1.13% FN (5/444); all were contacted and 80% (4/5) attended tertiary care. Over-reading, rather than adjudicated ground truth, defined false negatives.
links.quote: There were only 1.13% FN (5/444); all of them were contacted and 80% (4/5) presented at TC.

links.outcome: Median screening workflow duration per patient
links.effect: Median screening duration was 6:30 min with AI versus 5:38 min with manual screening, excluding patient registration.
links.quote: The median duration for a patient in the AI and manual screening was 6:30 and 5:38 min, respectively.
